newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Mass. officials took gifts from Goldman Sachs.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Mass. officials took gifts from Goldman Sachs.

text.p: The Massachusetts State Ethics Commission on Thursday fined Goldman, Sachs & Co $3,500 for feting two former state officials: a deputy treasurer, and the head of the Health and Education Facilities Authority (HEFA).

Goldman Sachs, which was the lead underwriter for about 25 percent of the $6.4 billion in bonds issued by HEFA between 1989 and 1995, said, "The firm cooperated fully with the state ethics commission and is gratified that the commission found no evidence indicating that the relatively modest amounts involved were intended to influence any acts by Massachusetts officials."

Neither Daniel McCarthy, a vice president at the underwriter's Boston Institutional Department, nor Larry Kohn, a vice president with the Asset Management group, nor Benjamin Wolfe, a vice president in the underwriter's municipal bond department are currently employed at Goldman Sachs, a spokesman for the firm said.

The commission fined former deputy state treasurer Steven Kaseta for taking theater tickets and dinners in Boston and New York from Goldman while he was on a committee in 1991 that awarded the investment banking firm a $400,000 fee to manage one of the state's equity pension funds then valued at $100 million.
Kaseta could not be reached for comment.

"Steve Kaseta left the office four years ago, but he was instrumental in taking the pension fund from the worst performing in the nation to among the best," said spokesman for Massachusetts Treasurer Joe Malone. "In this case, he made a mistake. He admitted he has made a mistake and he has paid a fine and we think that's appropriate."

The commission, in a public enforcement letter, to the former head of HEFA Edward Murphy detailed the growing friendship between Murphy and then-Goldman, Sachs municipal bond department vice president Wolfe through a series of dinners, lunches and family get-togethers that appeared to begin through their business relationship starting in 1989.

And while the commission could find no direct evidence that there was a quid pro quo between the men, "there is reasonable cause to believe that your acceptance of the above free meals and tickets of substantial value was for or because of offical acts...and that you there by violated (state law," the letter said.
Now at Tucker Anthony, Murphy through his attorney Thomas Kiley, noted he did "not admitted to the facts or agree with their interpretation of the law."
"We have agreed to disagree. There are no fines, no admissions, no liability. We're just going to move on."
